text: Which version of the code produced the number in Figure 3 is a question every research project eventually has to answer, and I'm not sure, I've changed the gate matrix a few times since then, is not an answer anyone can build on. Git exists to make that question always answerable.

It's tempting to think version control is overhead only real software projects need, but research code is exactly where you most need to answer what the code looked like when it produced this result. A commit message is most useful when it says why a change was made, especially when it affects a numeric result. A git tag lets you mark the exact commit behind a published number permanently. And when a bug fix changes a previously reported number, the honest workflow is to say so explicitly rather than silently overwriting it.

Compare fix bug to a message explaining that the previous version used the wrong projector by mistake, which silently flipped the target qubit when the control was zero instead of one, confirmed against the standard CNOT truth table. Both commits change the same lines, but only the second tells a future reader, including future you, what was wrong and why the new version is trustworthy.

git tag dash a, with a name like v1 point 0 dash bell dash fidelity dash result, marks the exact commit behind a specific published number permanently. Months later, git checkout of that tag reconstructs exactly the code that produced it, no matter how many commits main has had since. This is the version-control equivalent of documenting a seed and a tolerance from the previous lesson.

Chapter 6 is this course's capstone: planning a mini quantum math toolkit that pulls together NumPy linear algebra, complex matrix checks, visualization, and the reproducible, version-controlled workflow from this chapter.
